content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. The bird is raised in many climates, and its meat is prized for its mild flavor, moderate fat content, and high protein level. Chicken can be used in a huge variety of dishes, from soups and salads to casseroles and grilled preparations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
The skin is edible and, when cooked properly, becomes crispy and rich in collagen.
Breast meat is the most popular cut, but thighs, drumsticks and wings are also heavily used.
Chicken is a staple in many diet plans because of its low fat content, especially skin‑less breast.
Different cultures have signature cooking methods, ranging from deep‑frying to slow braising in sauces.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken delivers a large amount of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat (skin‑less breast)
items.content: Skin‑less breast meat contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The meat provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein content helps keep you feeling full longer, which can aid weight management.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter, so it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Bird protein allergy
items.content: A small number of people can develop allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Chicken sausages, deli meats and ready‑to‑eat dishes often contain high levels of salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Chicken skin is high in saturated fat; excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be grilled, baked, boiled, fried or stewed. Breast meat is common in salads, sandwiches and low‑fat meals. Thighs and drumsticks are ideal for roasting with herbs and spices. The skin can be crisped and added to soups or salads for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen chicken retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or a grayish color; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

cookie-butter-or-sugar-with-chocolate-ic.title: Cookie, butter or sugar, with chocolate icing or filling

content.title: About
content.content: A cookie made with butter or sugar and finished with chocolate icing or a chocolate filling is a sweet baked good composed of flour, butter or sugar, and cocoa mass. The dough is tender, while the chocolate layer adds a rich aroma and a crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate‑coated cookie recipes appeared in Europe in the 19th century.
Combining butter and sugar creates a light, aromatic dough.
Chocolate icing is often made from melted dark chocolate with a splash of cream.
In some countries the treat is called “chocolate biscuit” or “chocolate bar cookie.”
Cookies can be round or shaped into figures, making them popular for festive gift boxes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and carbohydrates in the dough quickly supply glucose, boosting energy levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and any leavening agents provide B1, B2, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The cookie provides magnesium, iron and zinc, supporting normal bodily functions.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: The sweet‑bitter balance of chocolate can enhance mood and reduce stress.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Butter and chocolate may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chocolate‑iced cookies are fairly calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with tea or coffee, used in dessert layers, crumbled over ice cream, or incorporated into tiramisu. For a softer center, warm briefly in the microwave so the chocolate softens.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to prevent the chocolate from melting. Avoid direct sunlight, which can alter the texture of the icing.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and tomatoes, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and tomatoes is a dish made from beaten eggs cooked on a skillet with added fat (oil or butter). Cheese gives a creamy flavor, while tomatoes add fresh acidity and vitamin C.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the oldest foods, consumed for over 6,000 years.
Cheese increases calcium content and improves the texture of the omelet.
Tomatoes retain some antioxidants, such as lycopene, even when cooked.
The fat used for frying enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Omelets are highly adaptable; you can change the type of cheese or add herbs to suit taste.

items.title: Rich in high‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Egg yolk and the cooking fat help increase vitamin D availability.

items.title: Contains lecithin
items.content: Lecithin from eggs supports liver function and the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene acts as an antioxidant and supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using a lot of oil or butter can make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolk contains cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Certain cheeses are high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk, stir in grated cheese and diced tomatoes. Heat a skillet, melt butter or oil, pour the mixture and cook, stirring gently, until set to your liking. Garnish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat on a skillet or in the microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Kamikaze is a popular cocktail made of vodka, triple‑sec (orange liqueur) and freshly squeezed lemon juice. It is known for its bright, sour taste and high alcohol content, usually around 20 % ABV.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink’s name comes from the Japanese term “kamikaze,” meaning “divine wind.”
The first Kamikaze recipe appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
It is often served in shot glasses, but can also be presented in a martini glass.
Variations include using lime instead of lemon or swapping triple‑sec for curaçao.
The cocktail is a frequent choice in bar competitions because of its simplicity and balanced flavor.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Lemon juice is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Citrus fruits contain flavonoids that have antioxidant effects.

items.title: High alcohol content
items.content: Kamikaze is about 20 % alcohol, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Lemon juice can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol may enhance the effects of certain drugs; consult a physician if needed.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Kamikaze is typically served in chilled shot glasses after shaking the ingredients with ice. Sip slowly to enjoy the sharp, refreshing finish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the components separately: vodka and triple‑sec in a cool, dark place, lemons in the refrigerator. The mixed cocktail should be consumed immediately, as the juice quickly loses its aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Plantain is a large, starchy variety of banana that is usually cooked before eating. When fried in vegetable oil it develops a golden crust, a soft interior and a slightly caramelized flavor. Plantains are a staple in African, Caribbean and Latin American cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantains are not sweet bananas; they are denser and higher in starch, so they are rarely eaten raw.
In some regions they are called “black bananas” because the skin darkens as they ripen.
Fried plantain is served as a side dish, snack, or dessert (e.g., “tostones” or “plantain fritters”).
Plantains are rich in resistant starch, which benefits gut microbiota.
In certain cultures fried plantain symbolizes abundance and appears in festive meals.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The starch in plantain is released slowly, providing lasting satiety and stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Plantain supplies vitamin B6, niacin and folate, which support energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C in plantain protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a healthy gut.

items.title: High calorie content when fried
items.content: Frying adds significant calories, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Banana allergy
items.content: People allergic to bananas may also react to plantain.

items.title: Oil quality
items.content: Using highly refined oils can produce trans fats; prefer olive or canola oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried plantain is served hot as a side to meat, fish or bean dishes. Slice into rounds or sticks, fry until golden, then season with salt, spices or a squeeze of lemon. It can also be added to salads or enjoyed as a snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw plantains in a cool, dry place for up to 5 days. After frying, let them cool, then keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Discard if a burnt odor or mold appears.
